mappings.note: Recall of the price named in 'The Ball Poem' ('a dime, another ball, is worthless'). Verse recall sits in C-E1.4; LO-1 is worded for prose extracts.
An identification question whose answer is stated in the passage it belongs to; the skill is extracting a named fact, LO-1, not interpretation.
Meaning of 'amiable' as used in the line. A vocabulary item under C-E1.1, not a character question, even though it describes the postmaster.
Fill-in of a stated detail - what in the letter moved the postmaster. Retrieval, so LO-1; the 'why did he reply' sibling is the LO-2 item.
The decision to reply turns on the postmaster's wish not to shake Lencho's faith - motive and the writer's point, LO-2.
The answer (money) is stated in the same sentence of the story; plain extraction.
Retrieval of the amount raised. LO-1; nothing about character or theme is asked.
The postmaster's contentment at having done a good deed is an inner state, so LO-2 rather than the plain-fact LO-1.
The absence of surprise is explained by Lencho's confidence in God - a trait, hence character analysis rather than retrieval.
How Lencho felt on counting the money is his reaction and mindset, LO-2; the amount itself is the LO-1 sibling.
Lencho's verdict on the clerks reveals his distrust of people - character, LO-2. Not C-E1.1: the word 'crooks' is not being defined.
Content of the second letter (the remaining thirty pesos, not to be sent by mail) is stated in the text; extraction, LO-1.
Authorship of the set text is a recall item about the literary work itself; C-E1.4 covers recalling, while none of the LOs reaches beyond the content of the extract.
Lencho's satisfaction once the letter was posted is an emotional state that follows from his faith, so LO-2 rather than LO-1.
Single-fact retrieval (the postmaster). LO-1.
Corn is named outright in the story; retrieval.
Asks the learner to characterise the setting (solitary, cut off) from a locational detail - inference about context, which is LO-2, not the 'where was it' retrieval of LO-1.
'Means that' - the task is to interpret a descriptive phrase about the crop. Inferring and interpreting language is C-E1.1; no theme or character is at stake.
Choosing the quote that captures the extract's idea is theme identification from a prose extract, LO-1. Not LO-3, since no evidence has to be composed.
What the letter contained is stated in the text; extraction of information.
Completes the story's simile about the field 'covered in salt'. Figurative language is covered only by the C-E1.4 competency.
Duplicate of the 'describe the house's location' item: an inference about setting and context, LO-2.
Duplicate of the 'Lencho's letter included' item; stated content, retrieval under LO-1.
Past continuous against a past simple time clause. A tense-form drill, so C-E1.3; no text comprehension is involved.
Third-conditional verb form. Grammatical convention, C-E1.3.
Present perfect with 'yet'. Tense accuracy, C-E1.3.
Present perfect with 'over the last 30 years'. Verb-form drill under C-E1.3.
Simple present for habitual action ('usually'). Grammar, C-E1.3.
Present perfect continuous for a duration up to now. C-E1.3.
Future perfect continuous ('this time next year ... for 7 years'). Tense accuracy, C-E1.3.
Quantifier/determiner choice across two blanks. A structural convention, so C-E1.3 rather than the vocabulary competency C-E1.1.
'Neither of' with two items - determiner agreement, C-E1.3.
'Both of' with a plural subject. Determiner and agreement, C-E1.3.
Perfect continuous form coordinated with 'have just finished'. Verb-form accuracy, C-E1.3.
Past perfect for the earlier of two past actions. C-E1.3.
Present perfect for a continuing stay. Tense selection, C-E1.3.
Future perfect with 'by the next month'. C-E1.3.
Subject-verb agreement with a measure phrase ('two dozen'). Grammatical convention, C-E1.3.
'Every boy and girl' takes a singular verb - agreement rule, C-E1.3.
Present perfect continuous with 'for a year now'. Tense accuracy, C-E1.3.
